props.title: Ontology
props.sub: the layer of meaning — a shared grammar machines can agree on

props.title: Not a schema. Not a taxonomy. A model of meaning.

left.head: Schema / taxonomy
rows: A database schema says how bytes are stored.
A taxonomy is just a tree of categories.
Neither one tells a machine what a thing MEANS.
Change the storage, and the meaning is lost.

right.head: Ontology
rows: Defines entities: Report, Query, Table, Service.
Defines rules: every Report must use ≥1 Query.
Independent of any one database or vendor.

props.foot: The ontology is the contract every source, every query, and every agent shares.

props.title: Everything reduces to a triple: subject → predicate → object
props.foot: Millions of triples, sharing one vocabulary, become a graph of meaning.

props.kicker: DON'T START FROM A BLANK PAGE
props.title: Most of your ontology has already been written

cards.head: Upper ontologies
cards.body: Generic building blocks for things, people, documents — schema.org, Gist, Dublin Core.

cards.head: Domain ontologies
cards.body: Whole worlds, pre-built: FIBO for finance, SNOMED for health, Microsoft's DTDL ontologies for buildings.

cards.head: Import & extend
cards.body: Pull in a standard vocabulary, then add only your project's specifics on top.

props.foot: Reuse buys you interoperability for free — and saves months of arguing about words.

props.kicker: OWL SAYS WHAT IS · SHACL SAYS WHAT MUST BE
props.title: Meaning you can reason on, and rules you can enforce
props.caption: OWL declares the concepts · SHACL validates every instance against the rules
props.foot: Machine-checkable meaning: the ontology can catch a broken model before an agent ever sees it.

props.kicker: REASONING · FACTS YOU NEVER WROTE DOWN
props.title: OWL lets the machine derive new truths from stated ones
props.foot: Declare the rules once; the reasoner keeps the derived facts correct for free.

props.title: The standards and tools you'll actually reach for
props.foot: Standards for portability; a good editor for the humans; a platform when you scale.

props.title: You use ontology-backed knowledge graphs every day

cards.head: Google
cards.body: The Knowledge Graph behind every search panel — billions of entities and facts.

cards.head: Amazon · LinkedIn
cards.body: Product graphs, and LinkedIn's ‘Economic Graph’ of people, jobs and skills.

cards.head: Health · Finance
cards.body: SNOMED for medicine, FIBO for finance — safety-critical shared meaning.

props.foot: Proven at planet scale. What's new is that a normal team can finally build one too.

props.kicker: HOW TO DESIGN ONE THAT SHIPS
props.title: The principles that keep an ontology from becoming a swamp

cards.head: Start from questions
cards.body: List the ‘competency questions’ it must answer — ‘which reports break if this table changes?’ — and model just enough to answer them.

cards.head: Small, then grow
cards.body: Twenty classes that earn their keep beat five hundred that never ship. Add classes when a real question needs them.

cards.head: Test-driven
cards.body: Encode the rules as SHACL shapes — your ontology gets a test suite, exactly like code.

props.foot: An ontology is software. Scope it, iterate it, test it — don't try to model the universe.

props.kicker: WHY AGENTS NEED THIS · THE DECISION-CENTRIC ONTOLOGY
props.title: Palantir's insight: meaning isn't enough — model the action too

cards.head: Data
cards.body: The objects and links — your report, query, table, and how they relate.

cards.head: Logic
cards.body: Derived facts and business rules computed over the objects.

cards.head: Action
cards.body: The typed, allowed operations — ‘open a work item’, ‘page the owner’.

cards.head: Security
cards.body: Who — human or agent — may see and do what, enforced at the meaning layer.

props.foot: So: an ontology is the shared grammar — and it defines the safe verbs an agent is allowed to use.
